article.overview: An atmospheric temperature sensor is a payload concept for measuring the temperature of the Moon's very thin atmosphere, which behaves as an exosphere rather than as a dense gas layer. No flown, prototype or proposed lunar instrument whose primary function is gas temperature was identified in this review. The nearest real instruments measure related quantities: the Apollo 17 Lunar Atmospheric Composition Experiment (LACE) measured gas composition with a mass spectrometer [1], and the ESA EMS-L instrument planned for the JAXA-ISRO LUPEX mission carries an infrared sensor that measures the temperature of the regolith in front of its aperture, not the temperature of the gas [2]. This entry therefore describes the measurement problem and the nearest instruments rather than a verified design.
article.description: A surface temperature sensor is conceptually simple: it is placed in contact with, or in view of, the ground and reports the temperature of that material. Measuring atmospheric temperature is harder. The lunar exosphere is so thin that its particles rarely collide with one another, so the gas cannot easily share its thermal energy with a sensor. A sensor placed in such a gas tends to settle at a temperature set by its own radiative and conductive exchange with the lander and the surface, not necessarily by the kinetic temperature of the gas particles it is meant to describe. This reasoning is general physics and is not taken from a cited source. The sources cited here describe the nearest instruments and their stated purposes. An instrument in this class would therefore need to define which temperature it reports (kinetic temperature of a given species, or an effective temperature), and to show how it separates its own thermal environment from the gas signal. In LACE neon analysis, densities were compared against a surface thermocouple reading [3], which illustrates how surface temperature is often used as a proxy when no in-situ gas temperature is available.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: A lunar atmospheric temperature measurement would aim to: (a) constrain the thermal state of the exospheric gas, which controls how readily particles escape or redistribute; (b) help interpret composition data, because a mass spectrometer's abundance results depend on the velocity distribution of the particles it samples; and (c) relate exospheric behaviour to the large day-night change in surface temperature. The LACE results show why a temperature parameter matters for loss processes: thermal escape was identified as the fastest loss route for hydrogen and helium [1]. These are proposed applications. No temperature-specific lunar atmospheric result was identified in this review.
article.operating_principle: No flown or prototype lunar atmospheric temperature sensor was identified, so no operating principle is verified for this entry. Three candidate approaches can be considered, none verified for the Moon. First, resistance temperature detectors (RTDs) in a slender probe, as used on the Mars Science Laboratory REMS air temperature sensors, where each sensor is described as a 35 mm rod carrying RTDs [5][6]. Second, thermocouples, which were used as a surface reference in LACE data analysis [3]. Third, a sensor that measures a gas-related quantity in a form that can be converted to temperature, a route that requires an independent physical model. The REMS experience is only partly transferable, because Mars has a far denser atmosphere in which the gas and the sensor exchange heat much more efficiently. That difference is engineering reasoning rather than a sourced result.
article.scientific_importance: Lunar atmospheric temperature is a missing constraint in any model of a very thin, largely surface-controlled atmosphere. Composition measurements from LACE and the planned EMS-L instrument need a temperature to be interpreted in terms of density and loss processes [1][2]. Without an independent temperature, mass-spectrometer results are harder to interpret. In the sources reviewed, the LACE mass spectrometer data had no available calibration, and a mass-to-charge ambiguity between singly charged masses and doubly charged heavier species was reported [4]. A temperature measurement would therefore help constrain the physical state of the gas, though it would not on its own resolve those instrument ambiguities.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a lunar atmospheric temperature sensor, and no flown example was identified. The examples below are related instruments: one lunar atmospheric composition instrument, one planned surface-regolith temperature sensor, and one flown Mars atmospheric temperature sensor used only for comparison. Values are given only where the cited source states them; otherwise they are recorded as null.

examples.name: Apollo 17 Lunar Atmospheric Composition Experiment (LACE)
examples.type: Historical lunar atmospheric instrument (composition, not temperature)
examples.status: Flown on Apollo 17 as part of the ALSEP package, Taurus-Littrow valley
examples.measurement_target: Lunar atmospheric gas composition and variation, mostly at night
examples.sensor_type: Miniature mass spectrometer (magnetic deflection type, per search summary)
examples.temperature_sensing: Not mentioned in the NTRS abstract reviewed [1]
examples.operational_duration: Ten lunar months of data collection, with operation limited in daylight [1][4]

examples.name: ESA EMS-L infrared temperature sensor
examples.type: Planned surface-regolith temperature sensor, companion to the EMS-L mass spectrometer
examples.status: Described as planned for the JAXA-ISRO LUPEX mission; flight status not confirmed in the source read
examples.measurement_target: Surface temperature of regolith in front of the EMS-L aperture, not gas temperature [2]
examples.sensor_type: Infrared sensor (principle not detailed on the source page)
examples.operating_range: Not stated; calibration is described as covering the extreme temperature range expected during the mission [2]

examples.name: Mars Science Laboratory REMS air temperature sensors (Curiosity)
examples.type: Flown Mars atmospheric temperature sensors, included only for comparison
examples.status: Flown on Mars on the Curiosity rover
examples.measurement_target: Air temperature near the rover, on a mast above the rover deck [5][6]
examples.sensor_type: Resistance temperature detector (RTD) rods, each described as 35 mm long [6]
examples.configuration: Two sensors on two short booms extending from the rover mast. The two are described as duplicates about 50 mm apart vertically and 120 degrees apart in azimuth, roughly 500 mm above the rover deck [5][6]

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No dimensions are published for a lunar atmospheric temperature sensor. The Mars REMS sensor's rod length of 35 mm [6] describes that instrument only and cannot be transferred to a lunar design.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: No mass is published for any of the examples. Mass would depend on the probe, its thermal shielding, mounting and the electronics, none of which is specified in the sources reviewed.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: No power figures were retrieved for the examples. Any heated or actively controlled sensor would need a power budget that is not specified in the sources reviewed.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: Any lunar sensor would operate in vacuum, across a large day-night temperature range, with radiation and micrometeoroid exposure. For an atmospheric measurement, the central requirement would be thermal isolation of the sensing element from the lander and from direct sunlight, together with a documented thermal model that separates the sensor's own radiative balance from the gas signal (engineering reasoning). The LACE operating record shows that the instrument was constrained during the lunar day because heating caused outgassing, so it operated mostly at night [4]. No lunar surface temperature range for this entry is quoted in the sources reviewed.
article.limitations: No flight-proven, prototype or engineering-model lunar atmospheric temperature sensor was identified in this review, so no performance values are stated. The physics of obtaining a gas temperature from a simple sensor in an exosphere is not resolved by any source reviewed (see Description). Even on Mars, with a much denser atmosphere, the REMS air temperature sensors are described as difficult to convert to true ambient air temperature because the mast sits above the rover's thermal plume and the sensors fall in sun or shade depending on the time of day [6]. The closest lunar examples measure composition or surface temperature rather than gas temperature.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: The sources do not define whether this sensor would be a surface package or an orbital instrument. The outline below assumes a surface package and is generic. No lander or spacecraft compatibility is assessed here.
transportation_process: Integrate the sensor into a lander or surface payload on Earth, with its sensing element positioned away from the lander's heat sources and exhaust.
Launch the lander or payload on a launch vehicle.
Land it on the surface and confirm a stable attitude for the sensor mount.
Deploy the sensor on a mount that keeps the sensing element thermally isolated from the lander and from direct sunlight where the design requires it.
Connect power, thermal control and data interfaces, then commission the sensor against a documented thermal model.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Not specified for this entry. The LACE instrument was deployed on Apollo 17 as part of the ALSEP package with its aperture pointed upward to catch gases descending to the surface [1]. That approach is a historical reference only.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: LACE on Apollo 17 is the main historical lunar atmospheric instrument identified in this review [1][4]. For temperature-sensing hardware, the Mars REMS air temperature sensors on Curiosity show a flown approach and the difficulties of interpreting its readings [5][6].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: Not assessed. No lander, rover or spacecraft interface was verified for a lunar atmospheric temperature sensor, so no compatibility is claimed.

article.historical_significance: No lunar atmospheric temperature sensor was identified as having flown. The historical lunar atmosphere record comes from pressure and composition measurements. Apollo 14 and 15 Cold Cathode Gauges are reported to have shown that a tenuous lunar atmosphere exists and to have set upper bounds on its density, but not its composition [4]. The Apollo 17 LACE instrument then produced a large composition dataset over ten lunar months, mostly at night, and identified thermal escape as the fastest loss route for hydrogen and helium [1]. Both results show that temperature is needed to interpret loss processes, but neither provides a direct gas temperature measurement.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
1. Existence: no flown, prototype or proposed lunar instrument whose primary function is gas temperature was identified. The payload name may describe a measurement concept rather than a specific instrument.
2. Definition: the temperature to be measured (kinetic temperature of a given species, or an effective temperature) is not specified in any source reviewed.
3. Data: no mass, dimensions, power, operating range, accuracy or lifetime is given for any lunar atmospheric temperature sensor.
4. Source strength: the LACE mass-spectrometer calibration point, the mass-to-charge ambiguity and the daytime outgassing constraint are from secondary summaries [4]. The surface-thermocouple comparison is from a search summary of an NTRS manuscript [3]. The LACE abstract [1] was read, but not the full PDF.
5. REMS details are from search summaries of the Journal of Geophysical Research paper [6] and a NASA/JPL caption [5]; the paper's page read returned no body text.
6. Ground-based spectroscopic temperature results for lunar sodium and potassium were surfaced in search but the primary papers were not retrieved, so they are not used here.
